claims.text: The baseline is a conventionally deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with relatively coarse grains and low grain-boundary density.
Lowering or otherwise modifying the deposition temperature can produce a nanocrystalline, grain-refined FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Grain refinement increases grain-boundary area or density.
Increasing grain-boundary density promotes deformation-twin nucleation over dislocation slip during high-temperature sliding.
Grain boundaries impede extensive dislocation motion and propagation.
Increased grain-boundary area facilitates the stabilization of microtwins.
Barriers to dislocation propagation localize strain and thereby promote deformation-twin formation.
Dynamic twinning can suppress strain localization and sustain more uniform plastic deformation.
Deformation twins distribute stress more uniformly and retard localized catastrophic plastic deformation.
Twin-mediated deformation enhances wear resistance in grain-refined FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
Relative to the coarse-grained baseline, the grain-refined coating will have a lower high-temperature sliding wear rate.
Relative to the baseline, the grain-refined coating will develop a smoother worn surface.
Relative to the baseline, the grain-refined coating will exhibit higher subsurface twin density during sliding.
Relative to the baseline, the grain-refined coating will exhibit lower subsurface dislocation density during sliding.
The proposed mechanism should hold below approximately 800°C while the FeNiCrCoCu coating remains phase stable.
High temperature activates softening mechanisms in high-entropy alloys.
At very high temperatures or extreme strain rates, other thermally activated softening mechanisms may dominate over the proposed twinning mechanism.
The quantitative changes in wear rate and twin density may depend on grain size, temperature, and sliding conditions.
Failure to obtain either a statistically significant wear-rate reduction or a shift toward significant twin formation would falsify the hypothesis.
